steps.explanationAfterStep: Hydroxide removes the OH proton. The alkoxide is now a strong internal nucleophile.

An intramolecular SN2 reaction: the alkoxide attacks the neighbouring epoxide carbon from behind, a new three-membered ring closes and the old one opens. The attacked carbon is inverted. The epoxide has moved one carbon along the chain. The app does not check stereochemistry yet.
Water protonates the new alkoxide and gives back hydroxide. Every step is reversible: the equilibrium favours the more substituted epoxide, here the 1,2-disubstituted one.

title: Payne rearrangement
subtitle: An alkoxide next to an epoxide: the epoxide moves along the chain
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 15

alkoxide.caption: the alkoxide + water
hintTiers: The alkoxide oxygen and the near epoxide carbon are close together. If the alkoxide attacks that carbon, what kind of ring forms, and which bond breaks?
The alkoxide attacks the epoxide carbon next to it, and that carbon's C–O bond to the old epoxide oxygen breaks. Two arrows: a new epoxide forms and an old one opens.
Alkoxide lone pair → new bond to the neighbouring epoxide CH; that carbon's bond to the epoxide oxygen → a lone pair on that oxygen.
alkoxide.learnerPrompt: The alkoxide is right next to the epoxide. Draw the ring-forming step.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Attack at the far CH₂ would make a four-membered oxetane. Three-membered rings close much faster: the alkoxide attacks the near carbon.
Taking the proton back from water just returns to the start. The alkoxide has a reaction of its own to do.

reactants.caption: 3,4-epoxybutan-2-ol + sodium hydroxide, in water
hintTiers: Hydroxide is a base as well as a nucleophile. What is the most acidic hydrogen in the molecule?
Hydroxide takes the proton of the OH group; the O–H pair stays on the oxygen, giving an alkoxide. Two arrows.
Hydroxide lone pair → new bond to the drawn H of the OH group; that O–H bond → a lone pair on the alcohol oxygen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Start with the fastest reaction of hydroxide here.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Hydroxide can open an epoxide, but only slowly. A proton transfer from oxygen to oxygen is much faster: deprotonate the OH group first.

primary-alkoxide.caption: the new epoxide with a primary alkoxide + water
hintTiers: The new alkoxide is on the CH₂. Which molecule can give it a proton?
The alkoxide takes the drawn proton of water, and the O–H pair stays on the water oxygen. Two arrows.
Alkoxide lone pair → new bond to the drawn H of water; that O–H bond → a lone pair on the water oxygen (hydroxide is regenerated).

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That reverses the rearrangement. Both directions happen (it is an equilibrium), but the reaction ends when the alkoxide is protonated.

mechanismSummary: Hydroxide removes the OH proton of the epoxy alcohol. The alkoxide attacks the neighbouring epoxide carbon from behind (inversion there), closing a new epoxide and opening the old one: the epoxide moves one carbon along the chain. Protonation by water gives 2,3-epoxybutan-1-ol. All the steps are reversible, and the equilibrium lies on the side of the more substituted epoxide. In synthesis, a nucleophile that opens the terminal epoxide faster than the other can pull the equilibrium across (Sharpless). The app does not check stereochemistry yet.
